raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old male with a past medical history of HIV (CD4 count = 537 cells/mm3, viral load <20 copies/mL) on antiretroviral therapy (bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide), hemorrhoids, and a recently diagnosed monkeypox virus infection, presented to the hospital with hematochezia. The patient has no history of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), diverticulosis, colonic polyps, or any prior gastrointestinal bleeding. The patient was tested for the monkeypox virus two weeks prior to this admission after developing painful anal lesions (Figure 1). The PCR test of anal and rectal swabs for monkeypox virus (MPXV) was positive, and he was started on oral tecovirimat (TPOXX) 600 mg twice daily for 14 days.
Prior to this hospitalization, the patient had recurrent episodes of bloody diarrhea at home for the last two weeks. Despite one-week tecovirimat (TPOXX) therapy, MPXV-induced proctitis progressed to severe rectal bleeding requiring transfusion. He had an episode of syncope and woke up on the bathroom floor covered in diarrhea and blood. Then, he called 911 (Universal Emergency Number) and was brought to the emergency department (ED). In ED, the patient was tachycardic and had a hemoglobin of 9.9 (103 g/microL) which was much lower than his baseline hemoglobin of 15.1 (103 g/microL) recorded two weeks ago. The patient's hemoglobin dropped further to 7.0 (103 g/microL) during this admission. CT angiography (CTA) abdomen and pelvis (Figure 2) revealed circumferential wall thickening with significant inflammatory changes at the level of the distal rectum and anus indicating proctocolitis. Two small, round hypodensities were observed near the distal rectum, with measurements of 11 mm and 14 mm. These findings raised suspicion of rectal abscesses.
Infectious diseases and gastroenterology were consulted and taken on board for further evaluation. Infectious diseases recommended continuing with Tecovirimat (TPOXX) and attributed bloody diarrhea secondary to monkeypox-induced proctitis. He had started on broad-spectrum antibiotics given the possibility of rectal abscesses. His hemoglobin stabilized after 1 unit of packed red blood cells (PRBC), and no further episodes of bleeding occurred, so no endoscopic procedure was performed. The patient was discharged eventually to finish his 14-day course of tecovirimat (TPOXX) and was followed up after two weeks with a resolution of anal lesions and no further episodes of gastrointestinal bleeding with stable and rising hemoglobin levels.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male presenting with acute, severe hematochezia and syncope following two weeks of recurrent bloody diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed painful anal lesions and recurrent bloody diarrhea over a 2-week period. Despite one week of oral antiviral therapy for confirmed proctitis, rectal bleeding progressively escalated into severe hematochezia. On the day of admission, he experienced a syncopal episode, awakening on the bathroom floor covered in blood and diarrheal fluid, prompting emergency services activation and transfer to the emergency department.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of chronic retroviral infection on antiretroviral therapy (bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide; baseline CD4 count 537 cells/mm3, viral load < 20 copies/mL); internal/external hemorrhoids; painful anal lesions diagnosed 2 weeks prior. Denied history of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), diverticulosis, colonic polyps, or prior gastrointestinal hemorrhage.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful anal lesions, recurrent bloody diarrhea, massive hematochezia, and syncope; negative for fever, nausea, vomiting, or abdominal surgical history. Home medications: bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide, tecovirimat (TPOXX) 600 mg PO BID. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Emergency department vital signs: tachycardic; blood pressure stabilized post-fluid resuscitation. Anorectal exam: painful anal ulcerative lesions. General: alert and oriented post-syncope; abdomen soft, non-distended.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline hemoglobin (2 weeks prior): 15.1 x 10^3 g/mcL (15.1 g/dL). Emergency department hemoglobin: 9.9 x 10^3 g/mcL (9.9 g/dL), dropping to an in-hospital nadir of 7.0 x 10^3 g/mcL (7.0 g/dL).
objective.advanced_workup: CT angiography (CTA) of abdomen and pelvis: circumferential wall thickening with significant inflammatory changes at the level of the distal rectum and anus indicating proctocolitis, with two small round hypodensities near the distal rectum measuring 11 mm and 14 mm raising suspicion of rectal abscesses. Endoscopy deferred due to stabilization after transfusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe hemorrhagic proctocolitis with suspected perirectal abscesses and life-threatening lower gastrointestinal bleeding secondary to monkeypox virus (MPXV) infection in a patient with well-controlled human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. MPXV confirmed by positive real-time PCR of anal and rectal swabs two weeks prior to admission. Diverticulosis, IBD, and colonic polyps ruled out by history and CT angiography. Management & Outcome: Continued on oral tecovirimat (TPOXX) 600 mg twice daily to complete a 14-day course, initiated on empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected rectal abscesses, and transfused with 1 unit of packed red blood cells (PRBC). Hemoglobin stabilized without further bleeding, avoiding invasive endoscopy. At 2-week follow-up, anal lesions had completely resolved, gastrointestinal bleeding ceased, and hemoglobin remained stable and rising.
